# m05-l03 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

Equilibrium Revisited.

An object is in equilibrium when the net force on it is zero, even if more than two forces act on it.

Our big question for this lesson: how can you analyze the forces on a train as it climbs a hill? So far, we've looked at motion along flat, horizontal surfaces. Now we'll tackle forces that act at angles other than 90 degrees.

When the net force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. By Newton's laws, it won't accelerate, so it moves with constant velocity. And remember, staying at rest counts as constant velocity. Equilibrium can happen with more than two forces too. As long as the net force is zero, the object is in equilibrium.

## Slide 2

The Ring in Equilibrium.

To show the net force is zero, add all the force vectors; in equilibrium they form a closed shape.

What's the net force on the ring in Figure 14? The free-body diagram shows three forces on the ring: force A pulling left, force B pulling up and to the right, and force C pulling down, the weight of the hanging mass. The ring isn't accelerating, so the net force must be zero. Because the ring is balanced, the vertical component of the force pulling up and to the right is equal to the weight of the hanging mass.

But you can't tell the net force is zero just by glancing at the diagram. You have to add all the vectors together. Figure 15 shows how. Place F sub A, F sub B, and F sub C tip to tail, and they form a closed triangle. So F sub A plus F sub B plus F sub C equals zero.

## Slide 4

Resultants and Equilibrants.

The equilibrant is the force that has the same magnitude as the resultant but points in the opposite direction, putting the object in equilibrium.

Now suppose two forces act on an object, and they don't add to zero, as in the free-body diagram of Figure 16. We want a third force that brings the total to zero and puts the object in equilibrium.

First, add the forces already acting. The single force that has the same effect as two or more forces together is called the resultant force. To put the object in equilibrium, add another force, called the equilibrant. It has the same magnitude as the resultant but points the opposite way. So the equilibrant is simply the negative of the resultant.

Look back at Figure 15: force C is the equilibrant of force A plus force B. Figure 16 shows how to find the equilibrant for two vectors, and the same procedure works for any number of vectors.

## Slide 5

Forces on an Incline.

On an incline, gravity points straight down, the normal force is perpendicular to the surface, and friction is parallel to it.

You've applied Newton's laws only to horizontal or vertical motion. How would you find the net force on the girl on the slide in Figure 17?

First, identify the forces on the system, which is the girl. Gravity pulls her straight down, toward the center of Earth. The normal force acts perpendicular to the slide, and kinetic friction acts parallel to it. You can see the free-body diagram on the right of Figure 17. And you know from experience that she'll accelerate along the slide.

Her weight is what makes her speed down the slide. If the slide gets steeper, so that the angle with the horizontal increases, the part of her weight that points along the slide gets bigger. That's why steeper slides are faster!

## Slide 6

Choosing a Coordinate System on an Incline.

On an incline, point the x-axis along the surface and the y-axis perpendicular to it.

Second, choose your coordinate system carefully. The girl accelerates parallel to the incline, so put the x-axis in that direction. The y-axis is perpendicular to the x-axis and to the slide's surface. This choice is smart because it lines the acceleration up with one axis, and it puts two of the forces, the normal force and friction, right along the axes. Only one force, the weight, has to be split up.

The weight has components in both the x- and y-directions. That means on an inclined plane, the normal force between an object and the surface usually won't equal the object's weight.

You'll apply Newton's laws once in the x-direction and once in the y-direction. Since the weight doesn't point in either direction, break it into x- and y-components before adding the forces in each direction. Example Problems 5 and 6 show how.

That's exactly how you'd analyze a train climbing a hill: tilt your axes to match the slope, then break the train's weight into a part along the track and a part pressing into it.

## Slide 7

Example Problem 5, Components of Weight on an Incline.

The components of weight on an incline are F sub g times the cosine of theta and F sub g times the sine of theta.

A 562 newton crate rests on a plane tilted 30.0 degrees above the horizontal. Find the components of the crate's weight parallel and perpendicular to the plane.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Include a coordinate system with the positive x-axis pointing uphill. Draw the free-body diagram showing F sub g, its components F sub g x and F sub g y, and the angles theta and phi. Known: F sub g is 562 newtons down, and phi is 30.0 degrees. Unknown: F sub g x, F sub g y, and theta.

Step two: solve. The angle from the positive x-axis to the negative y-axis is 270 degrees, so theta plus phi equals 270 degrees. Rearranging, theta equals 270 degrees minus 30 degrees, or 240 degrees. Then F sub g x equals F sub g times the cosine of theta: 562 newtons times the cosine of 240.0 degrees, which is negative 281 newtons. And F sub g y equals F sub g times the sine of theta: 562 newtons times the sine of 240.0 degrees, which is negative 487 newtons.

Step three: evaluate. Force is measured in newtons. The components point opposite the positive axes, down the slope and into the plane, so the negative signs make sense. And both values are smaller than F sub g, as expected.

## Slide 8

Example Problem 6, Down the Slide.

Sliding down a slope of angle phi, a equals g times the quantity sine phi minus mu sub k times cosine phi.

Ichiko, who has a mass of 45 kilograms, goes down a slide sloped at 27 degrees. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.23. How fast is she going 1.0 second after starting from rest?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Set up a coordinate system and draw a free-body diagram of the forces on her as she slides. Three forces act: the normal force, kinetic friction, and her weight. Known: m is 45 kilograms, phi is 27 degrees, mu sub k is 0.23, the initial velocity is 0.0 meters per second, and t is 1.0 second. Unknown: a, the final velocity, and theta.

Step two: solve. The angle from the positive x-axis to the negative y-axis is 270 degrees, so theta equals 270 degrees plus 27 degrees, or 297 degrees. In the y-direction there's no acceleration, so the net force there is 0.0 newtons. Adding the y-forces, F sub N plus F sub g y equals zero, so F sub N equals negative F sub g y, which is negative m g times the sine of theta.

In the x-direction, use Newton's second law. The net x-force is F sub g x minus friction. Friction is negative because it points in the negative x-direction. So m a equals m g cosine theta minus mu sub k F sub N. Substituting the normal force, m a equals m g cosine theta plus mu sub k m g sine theta. The mass cancels: a equals g times the quantity cosine theta plus mu sub k sine theta. The cosine of 297 degrees equals the sine of 27 degrees, and the sine of 297 degrees equals negative the cosine of 27 degrees. So this is the same as a equals g times the quantity sine phi minus mu sub k cosine phi, the usual result for sliding down a slope. Plug in 9.8 meters per second squared, 27 degrees, and 0.23: 9.8 times the quantity 0.45 minus 0.20, and a equals 2.4 meters per second squared.

Now use final velocity equals initial velocity plus a t: 0.0 meters per second plus 2.4 meters per second squared times 1.0 second, which is 2.4 meters per second.

Step three: evaluate. Dimensional analysis shows the velocity is in meters per second and the acceleration in meters per second squared. Both point in the positive x-direction, so the signs make sense. And 2.4 meters per second is about a person's jogging pace, realistic for a fairly steep slide with low friction.

## Slide 9

Engineering and Technology, Biomimetics and Friction.

Biomimetics is the application of ideas from nature and living things to solve design problems.

When engineers design solutions, they have to think about friction. Sometimes they want as much friction as possible, and sometimes as little as possible. Living things have offered clever ideas for both. Biomimetics is the use of ideas from nature to solve design problems. For example, burdock seeds stick to animals to travel from place to place, and scientists copied their structure to invent hook-and-loop tape.

To increase friction, look at the clingfish. It lives near the coast, where tides ebb and flow, and it has a suction-cup-like disc with an amazing ability to hold it in place. Friction is one reason the disc sticks so well, even when wet. The disc's outer edge is covered in hair-like structures so tiny you need a microscope to see them. Remember that when surfaces touch, their high points temporarily bond. Those tiny hairs vastly increase the number of contact points. Engineers can use this idea when they need to maximize friction, for example when developing adhesives.

To decrease friction, look at sharks. Friction can hurt the motion of vehicles and the function of machines. Shark skin is made of structures called denticles, and one of their interesting properties is reducing friction between the shark and the water. Using this idea in vehicles and machines could lower friction, reducing fuel use and energy consumption.

Now try it: draw a labeled diagram showing how biomimetics can increase or decrease friction. You might do some extra research to add details to your model.
